extracted.intended_audience: scientists, science communicators, journalists, and the general public interested in science communication
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and characterizing exaggeration and sensationalism in scientific communication across researchers, journals, and mainstream media, and understanding its causes and effects on public trust and decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'hype in science'
rubrics_metrics.description: Hype in science is the exaggeration and sensationalism of scientific discoveries when submitting discoveries to scientific journals and when publicizing results in the news media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core descriptor: look for inflated claims, sensational wording, and presentation that overstates novelty, impact, or certainty relative to the underlying evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive-motivation for exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Hype arises because scientists work in an increasingly competitive field where discoveries published by an individual have large ramifications on income and career; to make work stand out, many scientists exaggerate findings and embezzle their writing with affirmative terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, consider career incentives and publication pressures as causal drivers; assess whether language amplifies impact beyond what methods and data justify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased use of affirmative/exaggerative language over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies show the frequency of terms that may be used to affirm or exaggerate findings has increased in recent decades as academia and journal competitiveness increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative signals (rising counts of assertive adjectives/adverbs, superlatives, or overconfident framing) can indicate hype; compare wording against field norms and historical baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal selection bias toward exciting/positive language
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific journals are more likely to publish articles which use more exciting and positive language; journals themselves engage in hype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess editorial and publication practices: preference for novelty/groundbreaking claims, press-release tendencies, and whether editorial standards favor sensational framing over cautious interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of press releases and mainstream news in amplifying hype
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles with exciting/positive language are contenders for press releases and mainstream news articles; mainstream news media often utilize attention-grabbing headlines to gain viewership, which sensationalizes science to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace how a research article is translated into a press release and news story; identify amplifying changes (simplification, headline exaggeration, omission of caveats) that increase hype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hype occurs at every level with shared objectives but different methods/audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Hype in science occurs at every level of scientific publication (scientists, journals, mainstream media). The objectives at each level are mostly the same (attention, prestige), but the methods and audience differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate each actor separately (author, journal, PR office, journalist) for specific practices that introduce exaggeration; interventions may need to be tailored by level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientists' specific practices that constitute hype
rubrics_metrics.description: To gain a competitive advantage, scientists commonly exaggerate their findings or the ramifications of their findings; it is becoming increasingly difficult for scientists to have work published, which motivates exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for overclaiming of causality, overstated generalizability, omission of limitations, and use of promotional language in abstracts and conclusions as scientist-level hype indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals' specific practices that constitute hype
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals are more likely to select articles which present more innovative and groundbreaking discoveries, even if those discoveries are often exaggerated to the point of falsification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess editorial selection criteria, press release issuance, and marketing language; consider whether publication choices favor sensational narratives over methodological rigor or reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mainstream news practices that constitute hype
rubrics_metrics.description: Mainstream news media will often utilize attention-grabbing headlines, including new scientific findings, as a way to gain viewership; this leads to sensationalism of science to the public and eventual distrust in the scientific community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating news reporting, check for misleading headlines, omission of uncertainty, conflation of preliminary/uncorroborated findings with established knowledge, and lack of expert caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of hype on public understanding and trust
rubrics_metrics.description: False reporting of science can lead to a misinformed public making decisions based on falsified findings; the public becomes less trusting of scientific publications as more inaccurate or attention-seeking articles appear, alienating the reader from the scientific community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure impact by tracking misinformed behaviors, changes in public trust metrics, and engagement patterns; consider corrective communication and transparency to mitigate long-term distrust.
